articles.title: Animal rights group calls for ban at planned Oxfordshire theme park
articles.summary: Peta objects to any animal shows at Puy du Fou's proposed new theme park in Oxfordshire.
articles.body:
Animal rights group Peta have called on a local authority to block any proposals for a planned theme park from including attractions and shows featuring animals.

A decision on French firm Puy du Fou's proposals to build the history-based amusement park on land north of Bicester is set to be made by Cherwell District Council by the end of November.

More than 16,000 people have backed a Peta petition urging the council to reject any plans involving live animal exhibits or shows at the new park.

Puy du Fou said animals were often the "stars of our shows" and that those housed at the parks are looked after "to the highest international standard".

"Animals are not actors or props, and forcing them to perform demeaning tricks amid loud crowds, dramatic special effects, and relentless activity belongs in the history books," Peta's vice president of programmes, Elisa Allen, said.

"Puy du Fou in England can, and should, open as a fully animal-free park."

Although the exact contents of the proposed attractions at Puy du Fou's Oxfordshire development are not yet known, animals feature heavily in performances at the company's French and Spanish theme parks.

At its park in Les Epesses, in France, Puy du Fou features more than 2,000 animals in its historical-themed performances, including horses and birds of prey.

Responding to the petition, the firm said in a statement: "Our animals are the stars of our shows and we look after them to the highest international standard."

It stressed that its sites were all "properly scrutinised by all the relevant regional, national and international animal welfare institutions".

"Online petitions created by single-issue activist groups play no part in the statutory planning process. Particularly ones that are full of inaccuracies," it said.

"Perhaps if PETA had actually visited one of our parks and seen the care and love with which our staff breed, care for and train our animals, they might not have made such basic mistakes."

Under its proposals, Puy du Fou in Oxfordshire would include four period villages and 13 live shows in which visitors could "immerse themselves in British history".

Developers estimate the attraction could welcome up to 1.4m visitors a year once fully open.

The plans for the Oxfordshire park have sparked concerns from some locals , who have expressed fears about the impact the site will have on things such as traffic and wildlife.

But it has received support from local attractions and tourism bodies, including Blenheim Palace , Visit Britain and the performing arts and entertainment trade union Equity .

A decision on the proposals is scheduled to be made by Cherwell District Council by 30 November.

If approved, Puy du Fou has said it aims to open the park in phases, beginning in 2029. The park would employ about 2,000 people, the firm added.

articles.title: Teesside conservationists search for European eels in River Tees
articles.summary: The Tees Rivers Trust has been searching for eels to tag and track as they migrate out to sea.
articles.body:
Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration.

The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment.

The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs).

Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch".

The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda.

Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase.

"We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year."

The Eels of Steel project is funded by Natural England and the Tees Rivers Trust has been conducting the research alongside Hull University.

Each eel has a tag which emits a unique ping, which provides information about their movements while migrating.

The project aims to discover if the critically endangered animal is successfully leaving the river and making it through river barriers such as sluices and weirs.

Since 2008, European eels have been listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Numbers have declined by between 90-95% since the 1980s due to a range of factors including habitat loss, climate change and overfishing.

Ward said: "It is incredible to think about the journey these eels are embarking on, back to their spawning grounds in the Sargasso Sea.

"No-one has ever witnessed European eels spawning, they are a species that hold so much mystery."

The team say they are always open to suggestions for netting locations, particularly lakes and ponds, and ask people to contact them.

articles.title: BBC drama Shetland to return for 12th series
articles.summary: The new series will be made up of six episodes filmed in locations on the Shetland Isles and across Scotland .
articles.body:
The BBC detective drama Shetland is to return for a 12th series, with filming starting next year.

The new six-part series will see the return of Ashley Jensen, playing DI Ruth Calder, and longstanding cast members Steven Robertson as DS Sandy Wilson and Lewis Howden as PC Billy McCabe.

But DI Tosh McIntosh will be a notable absence because one of the original stars, Alison O'Donnell, leaves the drama at the end of the current series following a 13-year stint.

She has promised a "memorable" departure from the show, with the first episode leaving fans in suspense as she was left trapped in a locked water tank.

Further casting details for the next series will be announced in due course.

The show, filmed both in Shetland and at locations in mainland Scotland, averaged seven million viewers across 2025.

Anita Vettesse will take over as lead writer on the new series, which will be produced by Angus Sharpe and distributed internationally by ITV Studios.

The TV series, adapted from the novels by Ann Cleeves, was first broadcast on BBC One in March 2013.

DI Jimmy Perez, played by Douglas Henshall, was the central character for the first seven series, with Ashley Jensen then joining as DI Calder in 2023.
